subject: Polity
topic: Right to Information Act, 2005 — mixed tiers
description: Article 19(1)(a) basis, Public Information Officer, time limits, exemptions, CIC, recent dilutions

questions.stem: The Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005 derives its constitutional basis from:

options.option_text: Article 14, the right to equality before the law
Article 19(1)(a), the right to freedom of speech and expression
Article 21, the right to life and personal liberty
Article 32, the right to constitutional remedies

questions.explanation: Right to information is a corollary of Article 19(1)(a) — freedom of speech & expression. Settled by the Supreme Court in S.P. Gupta (1981) — 'open government is the new democratic culture' — and reaffirmed in Bennett Coleman (1973) and Romesh Thappar (1950). The 2005 Act gives this right a statutory framework. Distractor 1 — equality applies but isn't the source. Distractor 3 — Article 21 has been creatively expanded to include many rights but RTI's primary anchor is 19(1)(a). Distractor 4 — gives the remedy (writ jurisdiction), not the substantive right.

questions.stem: Under the RTI Act, a Public Information Officer (PIO) must respond to a citizen's information request within how many DAYS in normal cases?

options.option_text: 7 days from the receipt of the application
30 days from the receipt of the application
60 days from the receipt of the application
90 days from the receipt of the application

questions.explanation: Standard time limit: 30 days. SHORTENED — 48 hours if the information concerns life or liberty. EXTENDED — additional 5 days if the application is sent through an Assistant PIO; 35 days if the request involves data of a third party (consultation needed). FAILURE — automatic deemed-grant; PIO can be fined ₹250/day up to ₹25,000. Application fee: ₹10 for central / state agencies (no fee for BPL applicants).

questions.stem: The CENTRAL INFORMATION COMMISSION (CIC) is constituted under which Act?

options.option_text: Information Technology Act, 2000 (Section 79 onwards)
Right to Information Act, 2005 (Section 12)
Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 (entire scheme)
The Public Records Act, 1993 (under archives)

questions.explanation: CIC — set up under Section 12 of the RTI Act, 2005. Final appellate authority for RTI matters concerning the Centre + Union Territories. Composition (post-2019 amendment): Chief Information Commissioner + up to 10 Information Commissioners. Appointed by President on the recommendation of a committee — PM (chair) + Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha + Union Cabinet Minister nominated by PM. State Information Commissions (SICs) handle state-level RTIs.

questions.stem: The 2019 amendment to the RTI Act was widely criticised because it:

options.option_text: Removed the Act's applicability to private companies entirely
Let the Centre fix tenure and salary of CIC commissioners
Reduced the response time from 30 days to 60 days nationally
Excluded all state-government information from RTI requests

questions.explanation: RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 — the original Act fixed CIC commissioners' tenure (5 years or 65 years of age, whichever earlier) and salary (equivalent to Election Commissioner / Chief Secretary). The 2019 amendment empowered the CENTRE to prescribe the tenure, salary, and other service conditions of both CIC and SIC commissioners by rules. Critics: this compromises commissioners' independence — they now serve at the Centre's pleasure. Distractor 1 — false; the amendment didn't change scope. Distractor 3 — false; time limit unchanged. Distractor 4 — false; states are still covered.

questions.stem: Information that is EXEMPT from disclosure under RTI Section 8 includes:

options.option_text: Information about routine government office expenditures
Information that would harm sovereignty, security, or strategic interests
Personal addresses of public servants for service verification
Citizens' charters issued by central government departments

questions.explanation: RTI Section 8 — list of exempt information: (a) sovereignty, integrity, security, strategic, scientific, economic interests, foreign relations; (b) information forbidden by court; (c) breach of parliamentary privilege; (d) trade secrets, IP; (e) information from foreign government in confidence; (f) endangers life or safety of an individual; (g) impedes investigation. PUBLIC INTEREST OVERRIDE — Section 8(2) allows disclosure if public interest outweighs harm. Section 9 — copyright. Section 24 — bars certain intelligence agencies (RAW, IB, CBI for some matters) but NOT for corruption / human-rights violations.

questions.stem: Which Indian state passed a Right to Information law BEFORE the central RTI Act, 2005?

options.option_text: Kerala, in 1997 under the Janadhipathya Mission
Tamil Nadu, the first state to enact such a law in 1997
Gujarat, under the Sardar Patel Information mission
West Bengal, under the early Left Front government

questions.explanation: Tamil Nadu — passed the first state RTI law (Tamil Nadu Right to Information Act, 1997). Soon followed by Goa (1997), Rajasthan (2000), Karnataka (2000), Delhi (2001), Maharashtra (2002), MP (2003), Assam (2002), J&K (2004). The MKSS (Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan) led by Aruna Roy in Rajasthan was the most influential grassroots movement that drove the central RTI Act, 2005. Distractor 1 — Kerala had similar initiatives but the formal Act came later. Distractor 3, 4 — invented contexts.

questions.stem: Which authorities are NOT 'public authorities' under the RTI Act, 2005 (i.e., do NOT have to entertain RTI requests)?

options.option_text: Universities and research institutes funded by the government
Private companies with no government funding or substantial state aid
Public-sector undertakings owned by the central government
Local self-government bodies including panchayats and municipalities

questions.explanation: 'Public Authority' (Section 2(h)) — includes any body established by Constitution, Parliament/State legislature, or government notification; PSUs, government-aided NGOs, statutory bodies, etc. EXCLUDES purely private bodies. RTI does NOT apply to a private company unless it is 'substantially financed' or 'controlled' by the government. (BCCI was held a public authority in some HC rulings due to state recognition; Supreme Court ruled it isn't a public authority under RTI in 2018.) Distractor 4 — local-government bodies ARE explicitly covered.
